title: Odysseus: Journey and Loss
subtitle: The Odyssey's opening names a difficult return

odyssey.excerpt: Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide after he had sacked the famous town of Troy. Many cities did he visit, and many were the nations with whose manners and customs he was acquainted; moreover he suffered much by sea while trying to save his own life and bring his men safely home; but do what he might he could not save his men, for they perished through their own sheer folly in eating the cattle of the Sun-god Hyperion;

narrativeBlocks.title: A hero is introduced through travel
narrativeBlocks.body: The opening calls Odysseus ingenious and says he has visited many cities and learned their customs.

narrativeBlocks.title: The journey costs lives
narrativeBlocks.body: Verbatim opening from Butler's translation: “Tell me, O Muse, of that ingenious hero who travelled far and wide after he had sacked the famous town of Troy. Many cities did he visit, and many were the nations with whose manners and customs he was acquainted; moreover he suffered much by sea while trying to save his own life and bring his men safely home; but do what he might he could not save his men, for they perished through their own sheer folly in eating the cattle of the Sun-god Hyperion;”

narrativeBlocks.title: The crew's fate is not hidden
narrativeBlocks.body: The proem says Odysseus cannot save his men because they eat the cattle of the Sun-god Hyperion.

narrativeBlocks.title: An invocation sets a frame
narrativeBlocks.body: This is the Odyssey's opening in Butler's translation. It previews the poem; it does not replace the later episodes that show how each event unfolds.

narrativeBlocks.title: Return is not a simple victory
narrativeBlocks.body: The hero longs for home, but the opening also remembers crew members who never reach it.
